1.pericope_label: And the lot of the children of Joseph fell from Jordan by Jericho, unto the water of Jericho on the east, to the wilderness that goeth up from Jericho throughout mount Bethel, And goeth out from Bethel to Luz, and passeth along unto the borders of Archi to Ataroth, And goeth down westward to the coast of Japhleti, unto the coast of Bethhoron the nether, and to Gezer: and the goings out thereof are at the sea. So the children of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, took their inheritance.

schools.summary: Calvin notices that Manasseh’s remaining half is described at greater length than the whole of Ephraim, though Ephraim was larger, and attributes it to the extra matters Manasseh’s case involved, the settlement in Bashan and the ruling about Zelophehad’s daughters, while Ephraim’s bounds raised no dispute. He then asks how the tribe holding the birthright came to have towns inside its brother’s territory, and answers that Manasseh’s portion outran its population, so towns were deducted to make up Ephraim’s share. Gill notes that the lot went out of the urn next after Judah’s, government falling to the one tribe and birthright to the other, and takes Bethel and Luz as originally two places.

Henry explains the generosity of the lot from Joseph’s standing in his father’s house, and observes that the portion ran the whole breadth of the land through its heart, with a fertility matching the two dying blessings. His sharper observation is negative: this tribe alone receives boundaries without a list of cities, and the only reason he can offer is that Joshua belonged to it and may have been left to allot the towns himself, so that they never came before the council.

Clarke concedes that Genesis identifies Bethel with Luz and still reads them as distinct here, explaining the double usage by the site of Jacob’s vision lying near the town rather than in it, and illustrating from the way London can include or exclude Westminster and Southwark. He locates the border towns by distance from Jerusalem and glosses Ataroth-addar as Ataroth the illustrious, and he identifies the Arkite from Hushai, David’s friend. Wesley explains why the two tribes are treated as one in the opening verses and separately afterwards.

Keil explains the single lot as a device to keep Manasseh’s half from being severed from Ephraim, and sets out the order in which the chapter and the next describe the resulting territories. On the border he is the most exact of the witnesses and the most willing to be corrected: Bethel here is the hill range and not the town, so that Luz itself fell to Benjamin; lower Beth-horon is identified by its ridge and the wady dividing it from the upper town; and an identification of Ataroth that he had once accepted is set aside for another. He admits that the Japhletite is beyond recovery and refuses a tempting but impossible identification.

debates: Whether Bethel and Luz are one place or two, and what the name means here.
Why this tribe is given boundaries but no list of cities.
Why Manasseh’s remaining half is described at greater length than the whole of Ephraim.
How Ephraim, holding the birthright, came to hold cities within Manasseh’s territory.
Where Ataroth and the two Beth-horons stood.
outliers: Henry can offer no reason for the missing city list except that Joshua belonged to this tribe and may have allotted its towns himself.
Calvin answers the question about Ephraim’s cities by a calculation of population against territory rather than by rank.
Keil sets aside an identification of Ataroth that he had previously held.
Clarke illustrates the Bethel and Luz difficulty from the shifting extent of the name London.
Keil and Clarke independently fix the otherwise unknown Arkite by the single descendant Scripture names.
Gill observes that a place now unrecoverable was perfectly clear to the men whose border it marked.
themes: The lot of the children of Joseph
From Jordan by Jericho to the sea
The borders of Archi to Ataroth

5.pericope_label: And the border of the children of Ephraim according to their families was thus: even the border of their inheritance on the east side was Atarothaddar, unto Bethhoron the upper; And the border went out toward the sea to Michmethah on the north side; and the border went about eastward unto Taanathshiloh, and passed by it on the east to Janohah; And it went down from Janohah to Ataroth, and to Naarath, and came to Jericho, and went out at Jordan. The border went out from Tappuah westward unto the river Kanah; and the goings out thereof were at the sea. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Ephraim by their families. And the separate cities for the children of Ephraim were among the inheritance of the children of Manasseh, all the cities with their villages.

schools.summary: Gill separates the general lot from Ephraim’s own border, distinguishes this Ataroth and this Tappuah from others of the same names, and places the former four miles from Samaria, which is not where Keil looks for it. On the scattered cities he explains simply that Ephraim was much the larger tribe and needed more than its bounds contained.

Henry reports that the learned cannot draw this line exactly and that travellers cannot help them, the country having changed past recognition — cities without a footstep left, brooks dry, rivers moved. He then makes an editorial decision worth noticing: rather than raise doubts he cannot settle, he declines to raise them, resting on the fact that the border was perfectly clear when it was recorded and so did the work it was written for.

Wesley corrects the compass point to north-east, distinguishes the district of Jericho from the city that belonged to Benjamin, and states the chapter’s governing fact plainly: these descriptions are dark at this distance but were evident to the men who took possession by them. Clarke reports the upper Beth-horon as little known but near the lower, and identifies Tappuah as a Manassite city that named a district, which is the identification Keil argues against.

Keil describes the structure of the survey, treats the substitution of upper for lower Beth-horon as immaterial, and then shows his method and its limits: a second Ataroth inferred from the word went down but never located, a Naarath fixed from an old gazetteer, a Tappuah that cannot be the royal town because the resulting boundary would run north instead of west, and a second proposed site rejected on the same ground. He reports Calvin’s reason for the scattered cities, accepts it as possible, and qualifies it by noting that the same arrangement recurs where that reason would not apply. Ellicott reads the interlocking holdings as deliberate policy, binding the tribes by common interest, and compares the Roman testudo in which overlapping shields covered each man and his neighbour together.

debates: Which Tappuah is meant, and whether it is the royal town of that name.
Why Ephraim held separate cities inside Manasseh’s territory.
Whether the boundary touched the city of Jericho or only its district.
How far these descriptions can now be recovered at all.
outliers: Henry deliberately withholds the difficulties he cannot resolve rather than list them.
Keil rejects two proposed sites for Tappuah by the direction the boundary would then have to run.
Keil accepts Calvin’s explanation of the scattered cities as possible and then limits it, since the same arrangement occurs where it would not hold.
Ellicott compares the interlocking tribal holdings to the overlapping shields of a Roman testudo.
Gill and Keil agree that a second Ataroth is meant and place it in different regions.
Henry, Wesley and Gill converge independently on the point that what is obscure now was plain then.
themes: The border of the children of Ephraim
From Janohah to Ataroth and Naarath

10.pericope_label: And they drave not out the Canaanites that dwelt in Gezer: but the Canaanites dwell among the Ephraimites unto this day, and serve under tribute.

schools.summary: Gill declines to settle the cause and offers three: inability, with God withholding success on account of their sins; simple sloth; or covetousness, a trading people being unwilling to give up the profit of such neighbours, which he thinks the clause about tribute suggests. Calvin, as Henry reports him, holds that the tribute aggravated the offence rather than excusing it, since it shows the motive was gain, and since trading with them left Israel open to their idolatry.

Henry refuses the plea of inability and treats the verse as a brand on the tribe, laying it to carelessness or cowardice, to want of faith in a promise that would have carried a vigorous effort through, or to want of zeal for a command that required the Canaanites to be driven out utterly. He records a charitable reading, that the tribute was accompanied by a requirement to renounce idolatry, and then withdraws it on the evidence of what Israel afterwards became.

Clarke declines to choose between could not and did not, and adds the chronology: Gezer was not cleared until Solomon’s reign, and then by an Egyptian king who gave the captured city to his daughter. He closes the chapter by answering the sceptical use of unidentifiable places, arguing from English towns named by ancient writers and now lost, or moved, or renamed, that such changes impeach neither his own country’s ancient geography nor the sacred historian’s.

Keil reads the failure as inability rather than neglect, notes that the Canaanites remained in a condition of serfdom, and treats the notice as parallel to the one recorded of Judah, to be interpreted the same way. Ellicott makes the same connection in a sentence, that the failure of Ephraim is registered here as the failure of Judah was earlier.

debates: Whether Ephraim could not drive the Canaanites out or would not.
Whether putting them under tribute mitigated the failure or aggravated it.
Whether the tribute was accompanied by any requirement to abandon idolatry.
Whether places that can no longer be identified tell against the record that names them.
outliers: Gill offers three causes for the failure and settles on none.
Henry adopts a charitable reading of the tribute and then abandons it on the evidence of later history.
Clarke notes that Gezer was finally cleared not by Israel but by an Egyptian king, and given away as a wedding gift.
Clarke answers the geographical objection from lost and relocated English towns rather than from the text.
Keil treats the verse as the exact counterpart of the notice about Judah.
themes: They drave not out the Canaanites
